issue.title: Who pays when a leaseholder challenges a service charge?
issue.question: When a leaseholder challenges a service charge, who should carry the cost of the fight, and how fast should the new rules start?
issue.summary: On 11 November 2026 the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said more than three million leaseholders in England would get stronger rights to challenge unfair or unexplained service charges. From 1 April 2027 leaseholders can ask for charge information, and landlords need court or tribunal approval to pass on their legal costs of a challenge. From 1 November 2027 private landlords must use standard demand forms and give accounts and annual reports, with councils and housing associations following from 1 November 2028. The government says a Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill is due before Christmas 2026.

bench.title: Landlords pay their own tribunal costs; small landlords get forms
bench.answer: Keep the tribunal and the 1 April 2027 start, but change the cost rule. The housing ministry, through the tribunal rules, would make landlords bear their own legal costs of a service charge challenge unless the tribunal finds the leaseholder's case unreasonable [s1]. Leaseholders recover their own costs when they win [s1]. Small landlords get standard forms, so the paperwork does not bury them [s1]. Councils and housing associations keep the later 2028 date [s1]. We would know it worked if tribunal data show challenges rising, fewer leaseholders dropping cases over cost, and no rise in small-landlord complaints. Propertymark's survey found 89% of leaseholders say unfair charges are hard to challenge [s2].

bench.title: Let each building's leaseholders approve the budget before billing
bench.answer: The landlord stops being sole judge of its own bills. In each building, a leaseholder board, elected by the flat owners, approves the annual service charge budget before any demand goes out, and the landlord's agent reports to it. Landlords still cannot pass on dispute legal costs without tribunal approval from 1 April 2027 [s1], but disputes become rarer because bills are agreed first. Who: the government writes this into the coming Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill [s1]. How we'd know: fewer tribunal challenges, and the share of leaseholders calling unfair charges hard to challenge, 89% in a trade body survey [s2], falls. 31 simulated citizens backed checking charges before billing.

bench.title: Let flat owners steer the bills and share the fight
bench.answer: In this simulation, Parliament should start cost protections on 1 February 2027, ahead of the announced April start [s1]. Landlords must pay their own lawyers, without adding those costs to service charges. Leaseholders who win should recover reasonable costs. Each building should elect a leaseholder committee to inspect invoices and approve planned spending, with urgent safety repairs exempt. Committees could pool money for independent advice. Landlords should provide one simple account, with receipts available on request. No one should lose their home for withholding a disputed sum held safely until the ruling. After a year, measure corrected bills, dispute times and leaseholders’ unrecovered costs.

jury.question: When a leaseholder challenges a service charge, should landlords carry the cost of the fight or should the loser pay?
options: Landlords carry their own costs, always
Loser pays, with a safe harbour for small landlords
Leaseholders vote on budgets first, to head off disputes
jury.ruling: Landlords carry their own costs, always: the one who sends the bill should fund the argument over it.

reasons.text: I never understood these bills. If the landlord starts the fight, the landlord pays his own lawyers.
I rent, but I've seen mates stung by fees. Make the landlord carry it.
If the leaseholder is wrong, why should the landlord pay? Loser pays is fair, and small landlords need protecting.
Let the people who live there look at the budget before the bill comes. Prevention beats a fight.

minister.trial: From 1 April 2027, in the tribunal's service charge cases in one region, landlords carry their own legal costs and cannot add them to the bill. Leaseholders who win recover theirs. Small landlords with a handful of flats get standard forms and a named helper.
minister.fail_number: Fewer than 1 in 10 challenges end with leaseholders dropping the case over cost by the stop date, against today's 89% who say charges are hard to challenge.
minister.statement: Twelve simulated jurors said: the landlord sends the bill, the landlord pays for the argument. Fair. I'm signing a small trial, not a national programme. One region. Landlords carry their own costs. Leaseholders who win get theirs back. The trade-off: small landlords. A one-flat landlord is not a fund, so they get the forms and a helper. Show me it works, or we stop.
